column5: grass withers at YHWH's breath
column6: The commentary makes pasture's blackening an act of the One who produced it; Isaiah makes the grass wither when YHWH's breath blows on it, so decay remains within divine agency.

column5: fading grass and enduring word
column6: After the carried-away pasture the commentary places an unforgotten recitation; Isaiah sets the divine word that stands forever against grass that withers.

column5: all flesh as grass
column6: Peter reapplies Isaiah's grass to all mortal flesh, extending the commentary's grass image from pasture to human transience.

column5: abiding word preached as gospel
column6: Peter identifies the enduring word as the preached gospel, a Christian reading of the contrast the commentary makes between passing debris and a recited word not forgotten.

column5: YHWH dries green tree and makes dry tree flourish
column6: Ezekiel explicitly gives YHWH both directions of change, drying a green tree and making a dry one flourish; it closely meets the commentary's one hand that produces pasture and alters it.

column5: God causes grass to grow for cattle
column6: The psalm's praise names God as the one who grows grass for animals, supplying the same pasture-as-deliberate-provision setting before the commentary follows it into decline.

column5: God takes breath and creatures return to dust
column6: Within the same hymn, creatures die and return to dust when God takes their breath, supporting the commentary's rejection of an impersonal agent for life's ending.

column5: God sends breath and renews ground
column6: God's sending of breath creates and renews the face of the ground, giving the reverse movement to the commentary's dry-ground-to-new-pasture horizon.

column5: one God kills and makes alive
column6: The divine speaker says that he kills and makes alive and wounds and heals, a compact biblical analogue to the commentary's claim that the producer and changer are the same agent.

column5: YHWH kills, makes alive, brings down and raises
column6: Hannah's praise assigns descent into death and raising up to YHWH together, framing opposite turns of life as praise-worthy divine acts.

column5: God sweeps mortals away like a flood
column6: The commentary's flood carries loose vegetation away; Psalm 90 gives God the active verb of sweeping mortals away like a flood.

column5: morning grass fades by evening
column6: Psalm 90 makes grass flourish in the morning and fade and wither by evening, a sharply compressed season like the commentary's fa-linked pasture-to-waste movement.

column5: water-rooted tree that does not wither
column6: The water-retaining side of the commentary's flood scene finds a close counterpart in the tree planted by streams that keeps its leaf and bears fruit.

column5: chaff driven by wind
column6: Psalm 1 contrasts that rooted tree with wicked people as chaff driven away, joining useful rooted life to refuse that cannot remain.

column5: turbulent sea throws up mire and dirt
column6: Isaiah's restless sea casts mire and dirt to its surface; it is a direct scriptural water-and-refuse image for the commentary's floating guthāʾ.

column5: wild waves foaming shame
column6: Jude turns water foam into an image for condemned people, closely matching the commentary's move from flood debris to humans who become uncounted waste.

column5: chaff carried away with no trace
column6: The empires become threshing-floor chaff which the wind carries away until no place is found for it, sharpening the commentary's claim that dispersed debris leaves no reckonable remainder.

column5: ungodly hope as wind-driven chaff, frost, and smoke
column6: Wisdom layers chaff, storm-driven frost, and dispersed smoke to describe the ungodly's vanished hope, a Jewish analogue for guthāʾ as humanly worthless and gone.

column5: people scattered as desert chaff
column6: Jeremiah has God scatter a people like chaff before the desert wind, an exact judgmental transfer from vegetation debris to people.

column5: wheat gathered and chaff burned
column6: The winnower gathers wheat but burns chaff, providing the explicit selection scene behind the commentary's contrast of what is retained with what is discarded.

column5: straw and grain in a dispute about true word
column6: Jeremiah's question about straw and wheat occurs amid the true prophetic word, joining the commentary's refuse-versus-choice image to its nearby contrast between lost matter and preserved speech.

column5: rain makes earth sprout and yield seed and bread
column6: Isaiah describes water descending to make the earth germinate and supply food, the generative half of the pasture cycle that the commentary sets beside drying and loss.

column5: word accomplishes God's purpose
column6: The rain-and-growth comparison culminates in God's word not returning empty; this closely parallels the commentary's placement of an enduring spoken word after transient vegetation.

column5: teaching as rain and dew on grass
column6: Moses compares teaching and speech to rain and dew falling on grass, a precise meeting of the commentary's pasture and its immediately following recitation.

column5: passing heaven and earth, imperishable words
column6: Jesus contrasts the passing of heaven and earth with words that will not pass, making the commentary's grass-that-goes and word-that-remains contrast cosmic.

column5: cut tree still has hope of sprouting
column6: The commentary uses vegetation's emergence to open a resurrection horizon; Job grants that hope to a cut tree, setting up his deliberately darker comparison with a dead human.

column5: stump buds again at the scent of water
column6: Job's water-revived stump supplies the same rain, ground, and renewed growth image, but serves his contrast with the apparent finality of human death.

column5: a human dies and is gone
column6: Job immediately asks where the dead human is, the counter-voice to the commentary's use of plant return and re-emergence as a sign of being brought out again.

column5: dust-dwellers awake and earth gives up the dead
column6: Isaiah joins sleepers in dust to the earth's giving birth to the dead, directly meeting the commentary's move from soil-born pasture to human re-emergence.

column5: God opens graves and brings people up
column6: God himself promises to open graves and bring the people up, making resurrection an act of the same sovereign agent rather than a cycle without a hand.

column5: seed must die before it comes to life
column6: Paul's seed image makes apparent death a condition of new life, a focused Christian development of the commentary's vegetation-and-resurrection connection.

column5: God gives each seed its body
column6: Paul attributes the seed's embodied outcome to God as he wills, echoing the commentary's emphasis on divine agency across changes of state.

column5: perishable sowing and imperishable raising
column6: The sown-and-raised contrast applies plant language to the resurrection body, clarifying how a decaying earthly image can become an eschatological argument.

column5: all in tombs hear the voice
column6: Jesus locates the dead in tombs yet under a summons, a close Christian answer to the commentary's focus on those brought out after returning to earth.

column5: those in tombs come out to divergent outcomes
column6: The coming-out follows the summons and divides into life and judgment, adding explicit human accountability to the commentary's pasture and refuse contrast.

column5: earth and dust give back their sleepers
column6: 4 Ezra depicts earth and dust yielding the dead entrusted to them, an especially direct Jewish formulation of return from the ground.

column5: the earth restores the dead it received
column6: 2 Baruch treats the earth as preserving and then returning its dead, a useful counterpart to the commentary's contrast between what is carried away and what is held for return.

column5: ungodly claim birth by chance and nonexistence after death
column6: The book places an impersonal, no-afterlife account in the mouth of the ungodly, furnishing a Jewish counter-narrative to the commentary's rejection of time or chance as the final explanation.

column5: God clothes grass today and it is burned tomorrow
column6: Jesus explicitly makes God the dresser of grass while stressing its one-day transience, a close parallel to pasture under divine care and then rapid loss.

column5: rich person passes like a grass flower
column6: James applies grass's passing flower to a wealthy human, matching the commentary's shift from fading pasture to a judgment on those who privilege worldly life.

column5: scorched grass, fallen flower, perishing wealth
column6: The sun scorches grass and beauty falls as the rich person fades in pursuits, giving a detailed Christian worldly-life analogue to green darkening into useless remains.

column5: land drinks rain and yields useful vegetation
column6: Hebrews makes rain-soaked ground blessed when it produces useful vegetation, closely reflecting the commentary's water that stays with what benefits people.

column5: thorn-bearing land is worthless and burned
column6: The adjoining land becomes worthless when it bears thorns and ends in burning, supplying a judicial contrast to useful growth and retained water.

column5: grain falls into earth, dies, and bears fruit
column6: Jesus' grain moves through burial and apparent death into abundant fruit, a Christian reversal that makes explicit the regenerative possibility the commentary finds beyond dry ground.

column5: people as field grass and roof grass blighted before growth
column6: Isaiah renders defeated inhabitants as field grass and roof grass scorched before maturity, a specific human-to-vegetation judgment image beside the commentary's people made like debris.

column5: morning cloud, dew, chaff, and smoke that vanish
column6: Hosea's chain of vanishing vapour, chaff, and smoke makes Israel's idolatrous instability legible through the same dispersed-material imagery developed for guthāʾ.

column5: human days like grass and its flower
column6: Psalm 103 calls a human life grass and a field flower, a nonjudgmental mortality counterpart to the commentary's vegetal picture of the world's passing life.

column5: wind passes and the grass's place knows it no more
column6: The vanished plant leaves even its place without recognition of it, closely serving the commentary's secondary sense of refuse that no one counts.

column5: water-rooted tree remains green in heat and drought
column6: Jeremiah's tree sends roots to water and keeps green leaves during drought, giving the positive, held-water counterimage to floating and dried debris.

column5: parched ground becomes pool and grassland
column6: Isaiah reverses parched land into springs and grass, directly complementing the commentary's observation that barren ground can become the site of another emergence.

column5: rain satisfies wasteland and makes grass sprout
column6: God's rain satisfies desolate ground and causes grass to sprout, a creation-speech counterpart to the commentary's pasture emerging from earth.

column5: God's keys of rain and resurrection
column6: The rabbinic saying keeps the keys of rain and resurrection in God's own hand, linking the commentary's water, pasture, and return-from-death motifs under one divine agency.

column5: each blade of grass receives a heavenly command to grow
column6: This midrash reads grass's growth as ordered rather than self-explanatory, an interpretive counterpart to the commentary's insistence that pasture belongs among the Creator's works.

column5: seed buried in earth as resurrection sign
column6: Aphrahat's Syriac resurrection argument uses a seed's burial and renewal as a sign for bodily rising; it is a later explicit version of the commentary's vegetation-to-resurrection bridge, though the precise wording should be checked.

column5: God removes a vineyard's protection and makes it waste
column6: Isaiah's vineyard owner actively turns a cultivated planting into trampling and consumption, a close parallel to the commentary's claim that the producer also brings the pasture to its ruined state.

column5: God commands no rain on the abandoned vineyard
column6: The vineyard's briars and desolation include God's command to the clouds, making environmental decline a deliberate divine action rather than an impersonal season.

column5: God turns rivers and springs into desert and thirsty ground
column6: Psalm 107 gives God the reverse movement from water-bearing land to barrenness, directly extending the commentary's one-agent account of life-giving and drying change.

column5: God turns wilderness and parched ground into water sources
column6: The psalm immediately states the opposite turn, so its paired reversals illuminate the commentary's observation that dry ground may become the place of new growth.

column5: crop, vine, olive, field, flock, and herd all fail
column6: Habakkuk lists a total failure of edible vegetation and livestock, giving a particularly close pastoral scene for the commentary's loss of pasture and food.

column5: rejoicing in God after ecological failure
column6: The prophet's resolve to rejoice follows the failed pasture scene, making a biblical counterpart to the commentary's placement of vegetal ending within praise.

column5: green marsh plant withers before other vegetation
column6: Bildad's plant remains green yet dries without sustaining water, a precise counterpart to the commentary's attention to green still visible beneath darkening and to water's role in what remains.

column5: forgotten God compared with a perishing plant's hope
column6: Job applies the waterless plant's end to those who forget God, joining vegetal failure to the commentary's moral turn from pasture to human fate.

column5: chaff before wind driven by YHWH's angel
column6: The psalm combines chaff, wind, and an explicitly divine pursuer, sharpening the commentary's account of debris being carried away under a responsible agent.

column5: roof grass withers before it grows
column6: The enemies of Zion are likened to grass that fails before maturity, another human-to-vegetation judgment image beside the commentary's degraded pasture.

column5: unharvestable grass fills neither reaper nor binder
column6: The next verse emphasizes that the failed grass supplies no one, closely matching the commentary's secondary sense of residue that is not counted or retained.

column5: unabiding branch dries, is discarded, gathered, and burned
column6: Jesus makes a fruitless human likeness follow the full sequence of branch, drying, disposal, and fire, an unusually close New Testament transfer of withered vegetation to moral judgment.

column5: sleepers in earth's dust awake to divergent destinies
column6: Daniel directly answers the commentary's question of people being brought out after death and adds the same final division between contrary outcomes.

column5: God gives spirit, makes dry-bone hearers live, and sets them on land
column6: This continuation of the dry-bones vision joins divine breath, renewed life, and placement on land, completing the vegetation-and-resurrection horizon developed in the commentary.

column5: God revives and raises after deathlike judgment
column6: Hosea's compact revival and raising formula offers a prophetic human counterpart to the commentary's movement from an ended earthly state toward being brought forth again.

column5: world and desire pass, while God's doer remains
column6: The letter explicitly contrasts the passing world with the one who remains, closely matching the commentary's worldly-life versus enduring-reality contrast.

column5: water on dry ground paired with Spirit on descendants
column6: Isaiah fuses water for parched soil with God's Spirit for descendants, a particularly clear biblical bridge between renewed land and renewed human life.

column5: descendants sprout like grass by watercourses
column6: The human recipients of the promise sprout like grass beside water, making explicit the commentary's latent passage from pasture imagery to people.

column5: Creator gives breath and life again
column6: The mother grounds hope after bodily death in the Creator who first made all things and can give breath and life back, supporting the commentary's same-agent theology of ending and renewal.

column5: hearing Jesus' words and building on rock
column6: The commentary follows carried-away matter with a word that is not lost; Jesus similarly makes enduring stability depend on hearing and doing his words.

column5: rain, floods, and winds test the rock-founded house
column6: The flood cannot carry away the house founded on rock, a concrete Christian counterimage to the commentary's unrooted debris swept along by water.

column5: hearing without doing builds on sand
column6: Jesus contrasts retained, enacted speech with an unstable foundation, extending the commentary's proximity of remembered word and vanishing matter.

column5: flood and wind bring a sand-founded house to great fall
column6: The destructive water scene supplies the negative counterpart: what lacks a lasting foundation is swept into collapse.

column5: creation subjected to futility in hope
column6: Paul gives creation's transience a theological frame rather than treating it as mere accident, resonating with the commentary's attribution of vegetal decline to divine ordering.

column5: creation's liberation from decay
column6: The promised release of creation from decay gives a Christian eschatological completion to the commentary's reversible cycle of dry ground and renewed life.

column5: wicked sprout like grass only to be destroyed forever
column6: The psalm treats lush grasslike flourishing as the prelude to the wicked's final loss, a direct moralization of the commentary's green-to-dark transition.

column5: evil-doers quickly wither like grass
column6: Psalm 37 supplies a concise ethical application of withering grass to people whose apparent worldly flourishing does not last.

column5: God gives field grass for cattle
column6: The covenantal promise names God as giver of grass to livestock, another direct pasture-and-animal provisioning context for the commentary's merʿā image.

column5: God sends rain and makes grass grow in a hymn of praise
column6: This praise psalm joins rain and grass growth to God's care, supporting the commentary's framing of pasture among the divine acts that call forth praise.

column5: dust returns to earth and spirit returns to God
column6: Qohelet names both the body's return to earth and the spirit's return to God, an adjacent Jewish framing for the commentary's death, soil, and agency themes.

column5: denial of resurrection as a decisive theological error
column6: The Mishnah opening this discussion excludes one who says resurrection is not from Torah, offering a rabbinic counterpart to the commentary's attention to people who reject being raised after death.

column5: fire tests each person's work
column6: Paul's image of work exposed and tested by fire provides a Christian counterpart to the commentary's secondary claim that human works can be reduced to unretained matter.

column5: burned work brings loss despite the worker's rescue
column6: The distinction between a disappearing work and a person still saved sharpens the commentary's distinction between what is discarded and what ultimately remains.

column5: sea, death, and Hades give up their dead
column6: Revelation imagines even apparently holding realms returning their dead for judgment, an apocalyptic counterpart to soil or water no longer keeping what must be brought out.

column5: blackness named together with beauty
column6: The commentary stresses that ahwā's dark hue is not intrinsically ugly; the Song separately places blackness beside beauty, a tonal comparison rather than a direct botanical parallel.
